Modern.brandNameRationale: Two words. Draft List is what's on the tap wall, the brewer's daily selection. The brand sits on the smallest commitment the brewery makes: this is what we have today. Modern, plain, immediately legible to anyone who has stood at a bar.
Modern.industrySummary: Modern craft breweries are competing with thousands of others on the shelf and on tap. The customer has gotten more discerning and design-literate. Brand quality, can design, and a clear point of view do more work than they used to.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Other Half (otherhalfbrewing.com) holds the hype-driven peer. Trillium (trilliumbrewing.com) sits in the New England IPA tier. Hop Butcher For The World (hopbutcher.com) does the design-led aggressive middle. Modern Times (moderntimesbeer.com) has the strong visual world. We sit closest to Modern Times in posture.
Modern.positioningStatement: A small modern brewery with eight beers on at a time and no nostalgia.

targetAudience.primary: 25 to 45. Drinks craft beer two or three times a week. Already follows three local breweries. Will walk past four others to drink ours.

dos: Show the list and the prices clearly
Talk about the beer, not the founders
Use plain English on the menu
donts: Photograph the brewers with their arms crossed
Run a 'limited drop' campaign every Thursday

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark only. DRAFT LIST in a tight modern grotesk, all caps, two words on one line. A small geometric mark, a single thin underline, used as the favicon and on every can lid.

typography.primary: GT America for the wordmark and headlines
typography.secondary: GT America Mono for the tap list and prices

customSections.title: What it doesn't do
customSections.body: No 'crafted with passion' copy. No founder origin story on the can. No medals printed on the label. No 'limited drop' weekly hype.

customSections.title: Where it lives
customSections.body: A taproom with a printed list rewritten daily. Cans with the wordmark and the beer name only. The beer name and the ABV. Nothing on the back.

Modern.brandNameRationale: Almanac is a real word for a yearly farmer's reference book — listing crops, weather, festivals, planting dates. The name signals seasonal brewing without being literal about it, and places the brand in the lineage of modern craft breweries with editorial naming (Allagash, Trillium, Modern Times, Hill Farmstead) without copying any of them.
Modern.manifesto: Most craft breweries release a flagship and then a hundred 'limited' variants of it. We made Almanac because the actual interesting beer year is short and seasonal — six releases that match the calendar, brewed at the right time, sold while they are fresh. No flagship. No year-round IPA. The almanac is the menu.
Modern.industrySummary: Craft beer has matured into two camps: the year-round-flagship breweries (Sierra Nevada, Lagunitas) and the hype-release breweries (Trillium, Other Half, Tree House). There is a quieter opening in between for a seasonal-only brewery — six releases a year, brewed for the season, available until they sell.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Hill Farmstead (hillfarmstead.com) holds the small-batch farmhouse slot. Allagash (allagash.com) sits in the Belgian-modern peer. Modern Times (moderntimesbeer.com) is the editorial-modern reference. We sit alongside Hill Farmstead and Allagash, with the calendar as the menu.
Modern.positioningStatement: Almanac Brewing releases six beers a year, brewed against the seasons, sold while fresh.
Modern.positioningRationale: We strip the menu to six releases — one every two months. Each beer is brewed at the right time of year and ships until the cellar empties. No flagship, no year-round availability.

targetAudience.primary: Craft beer drinkers 28–50 who track release calendars and care about freshness.
behaviors: Subscribe to brewery release alerts.
Drink beer by season — saisons in spring, stouts in winter.
Visit the taproom when releases drop.
Trade specific bottles.
motivations: Want a brewery with a clear calendar.
Want fresh beer, not warehouse stock.
Want a small menu they can know completely.

dos: Publish the annual release calendar at the start of the year.
Write release notes like a farmer's almanac entry.
Reference the season, the weather, the ingredient.
Photograph the brewery floor, not the can.

messagingPillars.name: Six releases a year
messagingPillars.description: Six beers, one every two months. The annual calendar is published each January and held.

messagingPillars.name: Brewed to the season
messagingPillars.description: Each release is matched to the season — a saison for late spring, a märzen for early fall, a stout for January. The beer fits the weather.

messagingPillars.name: Fresh or empty
messagingPillars.description: Each release ships from the cellar until it sells. We do not refill the warehouse. When it is gone, the next one is two months away.

Modern.logoDirection: A wordmark — Almanac Brewing set in a calm modern serif with a small woodcut-style sun mark beside it. The mark feels printed, not designed.

colorPalette.name: Wheat
colorPalette.meaning: Primary — the color of an open field.

typography.primary: A calm modern serif for the wordmark and release names.
typography.secondary: A neutral grotesque for body and field data.
typography.rationale: The serif sets the editorial tone. The grotesque keeps the cans legible.

Luxury.brandNameRationale: Three words. Halewood is an English surname suggesting a long-running family brewery. & Co. closes it as a small heritage firm. The whole name reads as a regional brewery that has outlasted its founders.
Luxury.story: Halewood & Co. began as a single oak-vessel brewery in a market town. The current generation has stayed at the same address. The barrels have stayed in use. Some clients have been buying from the brewery for three generations.
Luxury.industrySummary: Top end beer has been moving toward larger craft brewers and bigger distribution. There's a parallel market for small heritage breweries in the older tradition. Few beers, old methods, oak vessels, decades-long relationships. The customer is paying for the brewery, the brewer, and the next pint in a decade.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Cantillon (cantillon.be) holds the institutional traditional brewery peer. The Kernel Brewery (thekernelbrewery.com) sits in the modern-craft heritage middle. Drie Fonteinen (3fonteinen.be) is the Belgian peer. We sit closer to The Kernel in posture.
Luxury.positioningStatement: A small heritage brewery making a few beers, very carefully.

targetAudience.primary: Wealthy, often beer-collecting. Has cellared bottles for years. Pays for the craft and the patience. Values the brewer's eye over the marketing.

dos: Address the customer by surname in writing
Name the barrel, the malt, the brewer
Send paper allocation letters

Luxury.logoDirection: A classical serif wordmark with elegant ligatures. A small hand-drawn ampersand becomes the brewery's hallmark, used on bottle labels, the cellar book, and the brass plaque outside the brewery gate.

Luxury.tagline: A small brewery in the Trappist tradition.
Luxury.brandNameRationale: A plausible Belgian abbey-style brewery name in the Trappist tradition (Westvleteren, Chimay, Rochefort). Saint-Cyran was a 17th-century French theologian — a real but obscure reference that reads as authentically monastic without imitating an existing abbey. The 'Abbaye' format places the brand firmly in the Belgian heritage-beer convention.
Luxury.story: Abbaye Saint-Cyran is a small brewery operating from a working monastery in continuous use since 1631. The brewery produces three beers — a single, a dubbel, and a tripel. Output is limited to what the abbey can produce by hand. The beers are sold in the abbey shop and to a small list of restaurants and bottle shops.
Luxury.industrySummary: Belgian abbey and Trappist beer remains one of the few categories where heritage and small-batch production are not in conflict. There is room for a small, faithful new entrant in the tradition — three beers, limited output, monastic register.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Westvleteren (sintsixtus.be) is the unreachable reference. Chimay (chimay.com) and Rochefort (trappistes-rochefort.com) are the Trappist peers. Affligem (affligembeer.com) is the licensed abbey-brand reference. We belong with the small Trappist and abbey producers — narrower in catalog, faithful in register.
Luxury.positioningStatement: Abbaye Saint-Cyran is a small abbey brewery producing three Belgian beers in the Trappist tradition, by hand, in limited quantities.
Luxury.positioningRationale: We do not scale. The abbey is the limit. The three beers have remained the same since the brewery's reopening, brewed by the same monastic community.

targetAudience.primary: Beer collectors and ecclesiastical-tradition followers who keep cellars and travel to the brewery.
behaviors: Travel to abbeys to buy beer at the source.
Hold mixed cases of Belgian beers across vintages.
Read about brewing tradition.
Pair beers with food slowly.
motivations: Want beer made in the tradition.
Want a brewery with continuity of community and recipe.
Want allocations they can plan a trip around.

dos: Sign correspondence in the abbey's name.
Reference the brewing community by tradition, not by individual.
Use specific brewing dates and pilgrimage dates.
Print all communications.

messagingPillars.name: Three beers
messagingPillars.description: A single, a dubbel, a tripel. The recipes have not changed. We do not brew a quadrupel.

messagingPillars.name: Made by the community
messagingPillars.description: Beer is brewed by the resident monastic community as part of the abbey's working life. The brewery is not a separate company.

messagingPillars.name: Sold at the abbey
messagingPillars.description: Most production is sold at the abbey gate. A small allocation goes to a fixed list of restaurants and bottle shops, by long-standing arrangement.

Luxury.logoDirection: A serif wordmark — Abbaye Saint-Cyran set in a classical book serif, with a small ecclesiastical crest depicting the abbey's stone arch. The crest appears blind-embossed on the label.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Single word. Tap is the smallest unit of a beer-drinking decision. The brand sits on the moment between standing at the bar and ordering. Plain, direct, and slightly anti-brand.
Minimal.industrySummary: Most breweries have elaborate names, mascots, and brand worlds. There's an opening for one that strips it back to the most basic word in the experience.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Most breweries fail this purity test. The closest peers in spirit are some Belgian Trappist breweries (where the abbey, not the brand, does the work) and certain Japanese sake makers.
Minimal.positioningStatement: A small brewery with three beers. No more. No less.

targetAudience.primary: Adults who don't need a brand world to choose a beer. They want a good lager, a good IPA, and a good stout, plainly packaged, fairly priced.

dos: Show the beer, the price, the ABV
Print the same label every batch
Use plain English
donts: Run a tap takeover marketing campaign

Minimal.logoDirection: A wordmark only. TAP in a single weight grotesk, wide kerned, all caps, three letters with generous space. No icon. The can, the menu, and the receipt all carry the wordmark and nothing else.

Minimal.brandNameRationale: Lot Seven names a specific production lot — the seventh batch run on the brewing schedule. The name is borrowed from the grower-producer tradition in wine and from numbered-batch industrial naming. Beerworks is a quietly archaic suffix for a small commercial brewery, less marketed than 'Brewing Co.' Together the name signals batch, output, plain trade.
Minimal.manifesto: Most breweries name their beers like racehorses. We made Lot Seven because the beer is a batch — Lot 142, brewed on March 6, ready on April 10. The label is the lot number, the date, the style. The brewery is named after the unit of work.
Minimal.industrySummary: Minimal labeling is well-established in winemaking and is starting to appear in beer. There is real space for a brewery whose entire visual system is batch numbers, dates, and styles — no can art, no series names, no flagship.
Minimal.competitorLandscape: Trillium (trillium.com) holds the well-designed minimal slot. Other Half (otherhalfbrewing.com) plays the modern minimal-edge peer. Hill Farmstead (hillfarmstead.com) is the rural-minimal reference. We sit further out — no decorative art on the can, just the lot.
Minimal.positioningStatement: Lot Seven Beerworks releases batch-labeled beers identified by lot number, date, and style.
Minimal.positioningRationale: We strip the can to a number, a date, a style, and a volume. The brewery is named after the lot. Each release is identified the same way.

Write back labels as field data.

Corporate.brandNameRationale: Three words. Eastside suggests a geographic identity and operational scale. Brewing Group names the holding-company category. The whole name reads like a real, established regional brewer-distributor already on the procurement panel at retail chains.
Corporate.industrySummary: Regional brewing and beer distribution is a serious B2B category. Retail chains, restaurant groups, and on-premise operators need partners who can deliver consistent beer supply at scale across multiple labels. The category is dominated by giants and a few specialist firms.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Anheuser-Busch InBev (ab-inbev.com) is the global giant. Constellation Brands (cbrands.com) holds the institutional peer. Boston Beer Company (bostonbeer.com) sits in the modern-craft scale tier. We sit smaller, focused on the regional contemporary brewing side.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Regional brewing operations and beer distribution for retail chains and restaurant groups.
Corporate.positioningRationale: Regional retailers and restaurant groups want partners who can deliver multiple brewing labels with operational discipline. The giants are too national. The boutique brewers lack scale. We sit in the middle.

Show case studies with retail-partner revenue

Corporate.tagline: Multi-brand brewing and distribution, regional scale.
Corporate.brandNameRationale: Caldwell is a surname with a Scottish origin and a hard, dependable register. Brewing Holdings signals the multi-brand operator structure with a holding-company suffix. The pair reads as a serious regional brewing operator with multiple brands under management — the kind of entity that owns three to seven breweries, a distribution network, and a hospitality arm.
Corporate.manifesto: Caldwell Brewing Holdings owns and operates a portfolio of regional brewing companies. Each brand retains its identity and brewmaster; we operate the shared distribution network, the back office, and the hospitality footprint. The buyer is a brewery founder considering sale, a hospitality group seeking distribution capacity, or an institutional investor holding brewing assets.
Corporate.industrySummary: Craft brewing has consolidated under a small number of multi-brand operators (Boston Beer, CANarchy, Tilray Beer). The opening is for a regional multi-brand operator with strong distribution, hospitality, and back-office infrastructure — at a different scale than the national platforms.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Boston Beer Company (bostonbeer.com) is the multi-brand scale reference. CANarchy (canarchy.com) holds the multi-brand craft peer position. Tilray Beer (tilraybeer.com) is the international peer. We sit in the regional multi-brand operator category.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Caldwell Brewing Holdings is a regional multi-brand brewing operator running breweries, distribution, and hospitality under a shared back office.
Corporate.positioningRationale: We compete on shared distribution capacity, hospitality footprint, and operational depth — across multiple brewery brands that retain their voice.

Creative.brandNameRationale: Two words. Pint Glass names the vessel of the social drink. The brand puts the shared experience in the brand position, not the brewer's ego. Loud, warm, and immediately legible.
Creative.manifesto: Most breweries sell the beer. We made Pint Glass because the actual product is the hour spent drinking it with people you like. The brand is for the round of pints at the end of a Thursday, the pub on the way home, the bar where you don't need to look at the menu. We brew good beer for the rooms where good beer matters.
Creative.industrySummary: Brewery branding has been polished, hop-forward, and slightly precious. There's room for a brewery that's loud, warm, sticker-friendly, and serious about the social experience of drinking beer.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Founders Brewing (foundersbrewing.com) does the irreverent middle. Sierra Nevada (sierranevada.com) holds the heritage peer. Russian River Brewing (russianriverbrewing.com) sits in the cult-craft tier. We sit warmer than all of them.
Creative.positioningStatement: A brewery built around the round, not the bottle.

Talk like the friend who's getting the next round

Creative.tagline: Beer for people who aren't quite locals.
Creative.brandNameRationale: Stranger is a real word — slightly literary, slightly Western, slightly cinematic. Paired with the working & Co suffix and Brewery, it reads as a small-town brewery with an outsider point of view. The name borrows from the bar-and-saloon naming tradition (The Drunken Devil, The Stranger's Rest) without imitating an existing brewery. Reads as warm and slightly mysterious.
Creative.manifesto: Most local breweries position around the town. The local IPA, the local lager, the local taproom serving the local crowd. We started Stranger & Co because the actual fun in a small town is being the new place — the brewery that opened on the wrong side of the river, in a converted barn, where the music is unfamiliar and the regulars haven't all decided what they think yet. The brand is the outsider in the bar.
Creative.industrySummary: Craft brewery branding has converged on either heritage-local (state flag, county map, town landmark) or design-modern (geometric can art, sans-serif wordmark). There is real space for a brewery that takes the outsider stance — slightly literary, slightly unwelcome, slightly cinematic.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Modern Times (moderntimesbeer.com) holds the editorial-modern slot. Half Acre (halfacrebeer.com) plays in the warm-creative middle. Burial Beer (burialbeer.com) sits in the dark-creative peer position. Mortalis Brewing (mortalisbrewing.com) is the literary-creative reference. We belong with Burial and Mortalis with a slightly warmer voice.
Creative.positioningStatement: Stranger & Co Brewery is a small craft brewery that positions itself as the outsider in town — literary labels, unfamiliar styles, a taproom that feels like a film set.
Creative.positioningRationale: The brand competes on tone. Cans, taproom, and voice all hold a single point of view — the brewery that came from somewhere else and is happy to stay slightly outside the town's habits.
